title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
OpenAI vs Google: the tide seems to be turning
Disclaimer: nothing has been decided yet, and my analysis is just a small glimpse of the status quo. The analysis is a little longer, but I look forward to your opinions and views. We are very welcome to discuss it.
@OpenAI and @Google have been fighting a tough battle for leadership in the field of artificial intelligence for a long time. As early as 2017, Sam Altman made it clear in an email exchange that he sees Google (DeepMind) as his biggest competitor in the fight for AGI. That other players would join the fray at some point was not foreseeable at the time. Anthropic, in any case, has shown that smaller players can also become big, and Meta, in turn, shows that they use “open source” (although it is not really open source) to avoid the Google route to acquiring market dominance (a free environment used by many that is an excellent fit for Meta's products).
Since ChatGPT conquered the consumer market in 2022, OpenAI has experienced rapid growth. Meanwhile, the term artificial intelligence is widely equated with ChatGPT. This is a leadership position that Sam Altman has worked hard to achieve – and Google was caught off guard and overrun. Their mass-market development was not yet ready, and they had to be made to feel it.
When ChatGPT had already built up a large fan base, Google tried to make up for its early mistakes with Gemini and to gain sales with the help of its products. However, the first iterations of Gemini were generally a failure, the miserable outputs a laughing stock (We remember that Gemini suggested that pregnant women smoke 2-3 cigarettes a day). Google lost the first round. Every product they released lagged behind OpenAI's development.
And so OpenAI didn't bother to overshadow every Google release by either releasing its own, usually better, product shortly before or on the same day, thus stealing the show from Google. Even in reasoning, OpenAI has so far been the leader. And nobody really understood why.
Because unlike OpenAI, Google has tons of TPUs for training and inference and even more training data to train their models (we remember Mira Murati, who was embarrassed and didn't want to admit that Sora was also trained with YouTube videos) and at the same time has an excellent research facility in DeepMind.
And DeepMind, in turn, consistently shows that they deserve the fame. Their products may have served the consumer market less, but they have achieved incredibly great results in the scientific field. AlphaFold has revolutionized chemistry, GenCast has provided a service for weather forecasting, and numerous other products have improved and promoted research.
But none of this helped in the consumer market. Google was left behind and even inferior competitors like Anthropic won far more admirers in the community. The only thing that set them apart was the large context window of 1-10m on the Gemini models. And at the same time, OpenAI has made big deals with news and news media outlets to get better quality training material and at the same time become the best news platform.
However, this month, out of nowhere, Google put OpenAI in its place. While OpenAI was using the 12 days of Christmas to present new products and developments, Google released models without prior notice, leaving many speechless.
Sam Altman, as former president of Y-Combinator, knows exactly how to make startups big. And a not insignificant part is “hype”. Through targeted leaks at Q* and ambiguous posts with strawberries, Altman fueled the community. Throughout the AI sector, there was only one company to look up to: OpenAI. And so these 12 days of Christmas are also a period in which OpenAI tries to get as much conversation as possible, to stay in the conversation every day. Sometimes it seems a bit silly when a whole evening is used to try to stretch the days with small improvements to SearchGPT that could easily have been presented as a blog update.
And SearchGPT also shows how OpenAI has partially overreached itself. SearchGPT is primarily an attack on Google's dominance in the search market. The search market is worth about $200b and is overwhelmingly dominated by Google. A search platform of its own like SearchGPT could do Google serious harm while strengthening its own platform. To that end, a chrome extension was also introduced that directs every search to SearchGPT first. But: it's bad. I tried it for a long time but uninstalled it again. It is not enough as a complete search replacement (when I have time I will write a long analysis about why I think the extension has done more harm than good).
So it was all the more shocking when Google, out of nowhere, released two excellent models, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Veo 2, without any advance notice. 1) Nobody expected them and 2) they surpass the quality of OpenAI. Gemini 2.0 Flash has several modalities, each of which is outstanding in its own right: text2speech with ginger latency, image recognition and an LLM (SLM) with excellent benchmarks and CoT approaches. Veo 2, on the other hand, beats Sora Turbo, which was released just a few days earlier – in many places significantly. It is clear that Google has had access to billions of hours of video material, so that physical demonstrations in particular are reproduced extremely accurately in videos. In short: Google is back!
And it did so without making a big announcement. And that's what I want to get at: as much as I understand that Sam Altman knows how to make good advertising, it can be exhausting and tiring to keep hearing about what might come next, trying to figure out what is cryptically written and understood as a hint at the next model (remember Orion, the starry sky in Sam's post) and as much as Google has shown how pleasant it can be when there is less talk and more delivery. And I hope that has given OpenAI something to think about and encourages them to deliver more than talk.
Please don't misunderstand: I think the world of OpenAI and I still think they'll be the first to achieve AGI, maybe even ASI. But they've also suffered numerous failures. The loss of Ilya Sutskever was probably the biggest. But it's time for OpenAI to show what they've got, too. Claude 3.5 Sonnet is still the best LLM in coding, and ChatGPT still hasn't been able to beat the model. Google has just shown with Veo 2 and Flash two models that outperform at least ChatGPT (but not o1) almost everywhere.
We all hope that GPT 4.5, a new model coming at the end of the week, will put OpenAI in first place. But last week showed two things very clearly:
1) The competition is alive, and that's good! It challenges OpenAI and forces it to work even harder.
2) In particular, OpenAI was embarrassed by Google by talking less about Google but delivering more. And that's something I would like to see from OpenAI from now on: less hype, more and better releases.
And I'm sure they can do it! Noam Brown is an incredibly great scientist and I think that with him in particular, you have all the opportunities for the future. But in the medium term, you should revise your advertising strategy, because in the long term it will become tiresome. In short:
OpenAI has everything it takes to remain number one. They can do it and I believe they will. But it's time to do more and talk a little less. That's all I want for Christmas.
Merry X-mas

It was an incredible experience contributing to LongVILA during my internship at NVIDIA, and I’m thrilled to see the latest amazing update led by @yukangchen_
LongVILA is an easy-to-use, full-stack, open-source solution from NVIDIA that enables building multimodal LLMs with 2M token sequence lengths (e.g., a 2-hour movie), based on Hugging Face’s codebase.
Exciting aspects of LongVILA:
1️⃣ Scalable infrastructure (MM-SP) supporting million-level context lengths in both VLM training & inference — also applicable on other modalities. 2️⃣ A data curriculum that uses the infrastructure to build true long-video LLMs with over 1M tokens in context, showing strong performance on benchmarks like VideoMME & Needle-in-a-Haystack.
🧵1/3

A full-stack framework co-designed for both algorithm and system optimization, enabling long-context multi-modal learning at an unprecedented scale.

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
I think the image metaphor of DeepSeek is incorrect.
Recently, there has been a lot of discussion about DeepSeek. Many people regard it as China’s first OpenAI-type company, characterized by a free research environment and a high concentration of talent. At the same time, some argue that DeepSeek is merely copying OpenAI’s model, believing that anything originating from China is often overrated or overhyped.
I don’t know much about them, but I had some early contact with them in early 2023. For various reasons, I didn’t end up joining them. However, from my limited interaction, I learned that they recruited a large number of medalists from NOI and ICPC. Based on fundamental technical skills, they are likely among the top in China.
Many of us are somewhat familiar with people who have competitive programming backgrounds. They tend to be both talented and hardworking. Beyond these traits, they often possess other admirable qualities. In my eyes, many of them are pure—purely driven by the pursuit of top-tier technical excellence. This drive enables them to ignore many trivial matters, such as peer pressure or office politics, and focus more seriously on creating something better. They find genuine joy in producing great work.
This kind of focus can be powerful. Many people, during their growth, lose the ability to pursue a singular source of happiness. They treat work as merely a means to earn money, or they seek validation through comparisons, titles, and accolades, caring more about external recognition than the intrinsic growth of knowledge and skills.
The stereotypes about Chinese researchers are understandable to some extent. Many Chinese researchers grow up from an educational environment that emphasizes intense competition. The activities people engage in during their formative years are often homogeneous, many examinations to prove you are better than others, and this homogeneity extends to research, resulting in a large amount of repetitive or incremental work. The metrics and rewards researchers face are also very narrow—often revolving around the number of papers published or whether a project has garnered some hyped feedbacks, like covered by media. These metrics aim to satisfy their supervisors, gain promotions, or secure better opportunities.
The scarcity of resources leads to fierce competition, which heightens anxiety and results in overlapping work or even overhyped efforts designed to attract attention and gain more exposure.
That said, I believe the internal environment at DeepSeek is likely different. Moreover, there are many exceptional Chinese researchers who don’t approach their work with this competitive mindset.
We should examine this new generation of outstanding young people with fresh perspectives.
We should also recognize that a good environment, a sufficiently diverse and rich talent pool, and an inspiring work atmosphere are critical for nurturing intelligence and innovation.
We should look forward to seeing more Chinese researchers producing outstanding work and contributing more exciting advancements to the world.
Quoting @archiexzzz
DeepSeek Engineers

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
my mum tried DeepSeek and told me she loved it because it could generate beautiful literature-level Chinese.
she has zero idea about which model is leading those AGI/HLE benchmarks, but she knows what model can best serve her needs in an easily accessible and affordable way.
maybe we should rethink what a good AI product should be like. I bet after several years, all the models will converge on those benchmarks. at the end of the day, every developer needs to answer "what special value can your model bring to users?" the majority of your users are people like my mum—they might choose gemini-2.0-thinking not because of its benchmark scores but because its explicit thoughts make her feel "wow, I'm talking to a human-like agent rather than a cold-blooded machine."
AI probably has no moat, but personality has.

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
Thanks to the great efforts of our team members!
Quoting @Leon_L_S_C
🌟 MMR1 Multimodal Reasoning Project Now Open-Source!
We’re thrilled to announce the release of MMR1, an open-source project dedicated to advancing multimodal reasoning research. The first milestone is MMR1-Math, a specialized multimodal model for mathematical tasks, achieving SOTA performance among open-source 7B models with only 6k samples from public training datasets.
🔍 Key Highlights of MMR1-Math
Open-Source 7B SOTA: Outperforms existing open-source 7B models on benchmarks like MathVista and MathVision, rivaling some closed-source large models.
Data Efficiency: Trained with only 6k curated public samples, proving the potential of small yet high-quality datasets.
Optimized Training: Leveraged GRPO reinforcement learning for efficient training (6 hours on 64×H100 GPUs).
Fully Open-Source: Models, datasets, and code are publicly available for rapid deployment and customization.
🌱 What’s Next?
MMR1-Math is just the beginning! We’re expanding to new domains (e.g., science reasoning), scaling to larger models (13B/70B), and advancing cold-start strategies and RL training recipes. Stay tuned!

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
We built sparse-frontier — a clean abstraction that lets you focus on your custom sparse attention implementation while automatically inheriting vLLM’s optimizations and model support.
As a PhD student, I've learned that sometimes the bottleneck in research isn't ideas — it's implementation. Want to experiment with sparse attention? You face a tough choice: modify HuggingFace models (easy but lacks parallelism support, requires patching each model separately) or navigate vLLM's complex codebase (supports tensor parallelism but has extensive, highly optimized internals).
🔬 What makes sparse-frontier special:
• Write your sparse attention pattern in 50 lines, not 5000
• Automatic compatibility with models supported by vLLM, support for TP
• 6 SOTA baselines with optimized implementations + 9 diverse evaluation tasks
• Research-grade extensibility for rapid prototyping
We used this framework for the largest-scale empirical analysis of training-free sparse attention methods to date (The Sparse Frontier) — which made evaluating across model scales (7B-72B) and sequence lengths (16K-128K) actually manageable. A key finding: for long sequences, large models with sparse attention outperform smaller dense models at the same computational cost, highlighting sparse attention's critical role in future LLM scaling.
🎓 New to sparse attention? Start with a companion repo, nano-sparse-attention, for pure PyTorch implementations and interactive Jupyter notebooks to understand the fundamentals, or our NeurIPS 2024 tutorial.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GtuYmUDWUAAz_Jc.jpg

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
Very well said…
Quoting @sainingxie
this isn’t just a modeling problem. it’s also a benchmarking problem.
spurious correlations are always a pain, but in multimodal llms they become a particularly tough battle. On one hand, you want to leverage the language prior to enable better generalization; on the other, that same language prior can turn into a shortcut that makes the model effectively blind.
the irony is that humans do the same thing. We still gravitate toward language-first tasks, and the “multimodal results” in major model releases like gpt-5 reflect exactly that bias.
I mean, economically this makes most sense for LLM companies: you can claim wins in “multimodal reasoning” without investing heavily in real multimodal research.
that shortcut will come due tho. when you try to put these systems into glasses, robots, or anything else that touches the real world, the cracks will show. and they’ll be costly.

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
Right after Sora2 was released, we ran an interesting comparison with LongLive, our open-source model released just two days earlier, focusing on long video generation.
Since Sora2 can only generate 10s clips, we used GPT-5 for prompt engineering, enriching the inputs with background & context to improve coherence. This experiment is essentially “a powerful closed-source video model + GPT-5 prompt engineering” vs. “a 1.3B open-source model designed for long videos.”
👉 Note: this comparison video is shown at 2× speed.
🎥 Sora2 shines in visual fidelity, camera motion, and physics simulation—far beyond LongLive-1.3B. We assume Sora2 has much larger scale & parameters, and we look forward to its technical report.
⚠️ With Sora2’s length limit, even with GPT-5 assistance, abrupt inconsistencies still occur between clips (e.g., in Video 2, Paul’s hair & mountain background suddenly change).
⚡ Meanwhile, LongLive-1.3B is faster. Sora2 takes ~3 minutes to generate 10s, while LongLive-1.3B runs at 20.7 FPS real-time on a single H100.
ℹ️ LongLive-1.3B was fine-tuned with our long-video extension strategy on top of Wan-2.1-1.3B (a strong short-video model), achieving real-time ultra-long video generation. LongLive is fully open-sourced, including training & inference code and model weights.

title: Fuzhao Xue (Frio) (@XueFz)
summary:
🚀📉 Efficient Inference Just Got a Major Upgrade
#NVIDIAResearch
We’ve just released Qwen3-8B-DMS-8x fine-tuned for 8x KV cache compression. It maintains dense model accuracy on demanding tasks like AIME24, and is perfect for inference-time scaling. The code on HF works out-of-the-box.
With DMS we fine-tune models end-to-end via distillation; this works much better than “token importance” proxies found in usual eviction methods. It’s state-of-art for KV eviction tailored for fast inference: adds negligible amount of parameters and computation to each KV head, and requires as little as 1K fine-tuning steps to reach 8x compression. It speeds-up both prefill and generation phase of Transformer LLMs, and can be combined with Sparse Attention methods such as DSA.
